name: Sushi
tagline: Vinegared rice topped with fresh seafood
summary: Bite-size vinegared rice topped with raw or lightly cooked fish and shellfish. Conveyor-belt sushi bars are cheap and fun, while counter-style restaurants serve an omakase (chef's choice) course. Many regions also have their own pressed or leaf-wrapped sushi.
local: Sushi is not only for special occasions. Supermarkets sell ready-made packs, and many families eat it as an everyday meal, saving high-end counter sushi for birthdays and anniversaries. Nigiri is a bite of rice with a topping pressed on top, gunkan-maki ("battleship roll") is rice wrapped in a strip of seaweed to hold loose toppings like salmon roe, and norimaki is a roll with the filling inside the rice and seaweed on the outside. Popular conveyor-belt chains include Sushiro, Kura Sushi and Hama-zushi.

shops.name: Sushi Dai (Toyosu Market)
shops.comment: One of the most famous sushi counters at Toyosu fish market. The omakase set is great value, but expect a long line.

shops.name: Umegaoka Sushi no Midori (Main Store)
shops.query: 梅丘寿司の美登利 総本店
shops.comment: Known for generous, high-quality sushi at reasonable prices. Lines are common.

shops.name: Sushi Zanmai Tsukiji Main Store
shops.query: すしざんまい 本店 築地
shops.comment: A big, friendly chain shop in the Tsukiji Outer Market, open long hours. Easy for first-timers.
shops.access: Tsukiji Outer Market, near Tsukiji Station

name: Sashimi
tagline: Thinly sliced raw fish
summary: Slices of very fresh raw fish served with soy sauce and wasabi, without rice. Coastal towns each have their own prized catch, such as seared bonito in Kochi and premium horse mackerel in Oita.
local: Sashimi is an everyday dish too: supermarkets sell fresh packs, and it is a standard menu item at izakaya (Japanese pubs). Near fishing ports, restaurants often serve it as a set meal with rice and miso soup.

shops.name: Uokin (Shimbashi)
shops.comment: A popular seafood izakaya chain born in Shimbashi, known for huge sashimi platters at fair prices.

shops.name: Tenfusa (Toyosu Market)
shops.comment: A market diner serving tuna sashimi set meals and tempura to market workers. Opens early in the morning.

shops.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
shops.comment: Not a single shop, but a market street full of seafood stalls and small restaurants where you can try fresh sashimi.

name: Ramen
tagline: Noodles in a rich, savory broth
summary: Wheat noodles in a hot broth, usually flavored with soy sauce, salt, miso or pork bone (tonkotsu), and topped with sliced pork, egg and green onion. Almost every region has its own style, which makes ramen one of the best ways to taste local food.

regional.ja: 青森味噌カレー牛乳ラーメン
赤湯からみそラーメン
長岡生姜醤油ラーメン
富山ブラックラーメン
宍道湖しじみラーメン

local: Ramen is casual, everyday food, eaten for lunch or dinner. As a national favorite, it is served by countless chains and small independent shops all over Japan, and supermarkets and convenience stores stock a huge range of instant ramen that many people also eat at home.

shops.name: Harukiya Ogikubo Main Store
shops.comment: A classic shop serving old-style Tokyo shoyu ramen since just after the war.

shops.name: AFURI Ebisu
shops.comment: Famous for its light yuzu shio ramen. Order from a ticket machine with English.

shops.name: Rokurinsha (Tokyo Ramen Street)
shops.query: 六厘舎 東京ラーメンストリート
shops.comment: A top spot for tsukemen (dipping noodles), with thick noodles and a rich pork-and-fish broth.

name: Tempura
tagline: Light, crispy battered seafood and vegetables
summary: Shrimp, fish and seasonal vegetables coated in a thin batter and deep-fried until light and crispy. It is dipped in a light broth or sprinkled with salt, and is also served on rice as tendon.

regional.ja: サクラエビのかき揚げ

local: Many families make tempura at home or buy it ready-made at the supermarket. It is also a common side dish with soba and udon, while high-end tempura restaurants fry each piece in front of you at the counter.

shops.name: Tempura Tsunahachi Shinjuku Main Store
shops.query: 天ぷら新宿つな八 総本店
shops.comment: A long-established tempura shop with reasonable lunch sets, fried in front of you at the counter.

shops.name: Funabashiya Shinjuku Main Store
shops.query: 天ぷら 船橋屋 新宿本店
shops.comment: A long-established tempura restaurant in Shinjuku with a calm, traditional atmosphere.

shops.name: Ginza Tenkuni
shops.comment: A tempura restaurant in Ginza since the Meiji era, known for its tendon and tempura set meals.

name: Soba
tagline: Buckwheat noodles, hot or cold
summary: Thin noodles made from buckwheat flour, eaten cold with a dipping sauce or hot in broth. Mountain areas with cool climates are famous for fragrant handmade soba.
local: Zaru soba is served cold on a bamboo tray with a dipping sauce, and many shops let you choose a plain sauce, one with duck, or a curry-flavored one. Kake soba comes in hot broth, often topped with mountain vegetables, mushrooms or tempura. Soba chains are found near many train stations, such as Fuji Soba and Hakone Soba in the Tokyo area. People also cook dried soba at home, and instant cup soba is easy to find.

shops.name: Kanda Yabu Soba
shops.comment: One of Tokyo's most famous old soba shops, known for green-tinted noodles and a strong dipping sauce.

shops.name: Kanda Matsuya
shops.comment: A classic soba shop in a historic building. Try the zaru soba or the duck soba.

shops.name: Muromachi Sunaba
shops.comment: An old soba shop in Nihonbashi said to be where tenzaru (cold soba with tempura) was born.

name: Udon
tagline: Thick, chewy wheat noodles
summary: Thick wheat noodles with a soft, chewy texture, served in a mild broth or with a dipping sauce. Many regions have their own style, from thin and silky to flat and wide, or simmered in miso.
local: Kagawa Prefecture, known as the "Udon Prefecture," has by far the most udon shops per person in Japan and many ways to eat it. The broth also differs by region: in the Kanto area (around Tokyo) it is dark and soy-based, while in Kansai (around Osaka and Kyoto) it is light golden and dashi-based. Outside Kagawa, udon is usually served hot in broth (kake udon), and sometimes cold with a dipping sauce (zaru udon). Tempura is a popular side, and people often cook dried or frozen udon at home. For Sanuki-style udon outside Kagawa, try the Marugame Seimen chain.

shops.name: Udon Maruka
shops.comment: Often called one of the best Sanuki-style udon shops in Tokyo. Firm, chewy noodles and a long line at lunch.

shops.name: Udon Shin
shops.comment: Freshly made udon cut to order. Famous for its butter-and-egg udon.

shops.name: Sanuki Udon Taniya
shops.comment: Udon made by a chef trained in Kagawa, the home of Sanuki udon. You can watch noodles being made through the glass.

name: Tonkatsu
tagline: Crispy breaded pork cutlet
summary: A thick pork cutlet coated in panko breadcrumbs and deep-fried, served with shredded cabbage, rice, miso soup and a thick, fruity sauce. Regional versions use miso sauce or come on rice as katsudon.
local: Tonkatsu comes in different cuts, such as fatty loin (rosu) and lean fillet (hire), each with its own flavor and texture. It is also an everyday home-cooked dish, and you can buy it ready-made at supermarkets and at butcher shops in local shopping streets.

shops.name: Tonkatsu Maisen Aoyama Main Store
shops.query: とんかつ まい泉 青山本店
shops.comment: Famous for very tender tonkatsu, served in a former bathhouse building.

shops.name: Tonkatsu Isen Main Store
shops.query: とんかつ 井泉 本店
shops.comment: Said to be where soft tonkatsu that can be cut with chopsticks began. Also known for katsu sandwiches.

shops.name: Tonkatsu Marugo
shops.comment: A popular tonkatsu shop in Akihabara with thick, juicy cutlets.

name: Yakitori
tagline: Grilled chicken skewers
summary: Bite-size pieces of chicken grilled on skewers over charcoal and seasoned with salt or a sweet soy glaze. It is a classic at izakaya (Japanese pubs) and goes well with beer.
local: Besides chicken thigh, yakitori shops grill skin, organs and many other parts, as well as vegetables. Basic yakitori is also sold at supermarkets and convenience stores, and frozen yakitori heated in the microwave is common at home. In the Tokyo area, Noge in Yokohama is packed with yakitori bars. In Fukuoka, try Hakata-style torikawa: chicken skin wound around a skewer and grilled repeatedly until crispy — it is well worth trying.

shops.name: Isehiro Kyobashi Main Store
shops.comment: A yakitori shop since the Taisho era. The lunch bowl topped with five kinds of skewers is popular.

shops.name: Torigin Ginza Main Store
shops.comment: A casual, old yakitori shop in Ginza, also known for kamameshi (rice cooked in a small pot).

shops.name: Omoide Yokocho (Shinjuku)
shops.comment: Not a single shop, but a narrow alley packed with tiny yakitori bars full of old Tokyo atmosphere.

name: Okonomiyaki
tagline: Savory pancake cooked on a griddle
summary: A savory pancake of batter, cabbage and pork or seafood, cooked on a hot iron griddle and topped with sauce, mayonnaise and bonito flakes. Osaka mixes everything together, while Hiroshima layers it with noodles.
local: Okonomiyaki is soul food in Osaka and the wider Kansai region. Families all over Japan also cook it at home on a hot plate, and supermarkets sell okonomiyaki mixes and ready-made ones.

shops.name: Asakusa Sometaro
shops.comment: A historic okonomiyaki shop where you cook at your own table. Staff will help first-timers.

shops.name: Hiroshima Okonomiyaki Denko Sekka (Tokyo Station)
shops.comment: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, layered with noodles, cooked for you on the grill.

shops.name: Chibo Ikebukuro
shops.comment: An Osaka-style okonomiyaki chain. Staff cook it for you on the hot plate.
shops.access: Seibu Ikebukuro department store, Ikebukuro Station

name: Takoyaki
tagline: Octopus balls from Osaka
summary: Round balls of batter with a piece of octopus inside, cooked in a special molded pan and topped with sauce, mayonnaise and bonito flakes. Crispy outside and soft inside, it is Osaka's favorite street food.
local: Takoyaki is Osaka's soul food and is eaten all over Japan. It is a standard at festival food stalls, and it is often said that almost every Osaka household owns a takoyaki pan. Tokyo-style takoyaki, made famous by the Tsukiji Gindaco chain often found in food courts, is cooked with plenty of oil so the outside turns extra crispy.

shops.name: Gindaco
shops.comment: Japan's biggest takoyaki chain, with shops at stations and malls all over Tokyo. Crispy outside and soft inside.

shops.name: Takoyaki Juhachiban
shops.query: たこ焼き 十八番 麻布十番
shops.comment: A small, popular takeaway takoyaki stand in Azabu-Juban.

shops.name: Odaiba Takoyaki Museum
shops.query: お台場たこ焼きミュージアム
shops.comment: A food court with several famous takoyaki shops from Osaka, so you can compare styles.
shops.access: DECKS Tokyo Beach, near Odaiba-kaihinkoen Station

name: Gyoza
tagline: Pan-fried dumplings
summary: Thin dumplings filled with minced pork, cabbage and garlic, pan-fried until crispy on the bottom. Utsunomiya and Hamamatsu compete for the title of Japan's gyoza capital.
local: Many families make gyoza at home, and supermarkets sell frozen gyoza that cook easily in a frying pan. Gyoza are mainly served at izakaya and Chinese restaurants, and well-known chains include Gyoza no Ohsho and Osaka Ohsho.

shops.name: Kameido Gyoza Main Store
shops.comment: A long-running gyoza-only shop. Plates keep coming until you say stop; you must order at least two plates.

shops.name: Nihao Main Store (Kamata)
shops.query: 你好 本店 蒲田
shops.comment: Kamata is famous for hanetsuki gyoza (gyoza with a crispy 'wing'), and this is one of its best-known shops.

shops.name: Kankei (Kamata)
shops.query: 歓迎 本店 蒲田
shops.comment: Another famous hanetsuki gyoza shop in Kamata, run by a family related to Nihao.

name: Nikuman (steamed buns)
tagline: Fluffy steamed buns with a savory filling
summary: Soft, fluffy steamed buns filled with juicy minced pork and onion. Sold hot at convenience stores in winter, and in Chinatowns and specialty shops all year round. Fun variations include pizza buns with tomato sauce and cheese, and seafood or curry fillings.

shops.name: Bonna Shinjuku Nakamuraya
shops.comment: Nakamuraya is said to be the first company in Japan to sell chuka-man (steamed buns). The shop sells buns and sweets.

shops.name: Raya Tokyo Butaman (Shinagawa)
shops.query: 羅家 東京豚饅 品川
shops.comment: A butaman shop started by the grandson of the founder of Osaka's famous 551 Horai.

shops.name: Lukang (Sakura-shinmachi)
shops.comment: A small shop making Taiwanese-style meat buns by hand.

name: Japanese curry
tagline: Mild, thick curry on rice
summary: A thick, mildly spiced curry with meat and vegetables served over rice, often with a pork cutlet on top. It is one of Japan's most popular everyday meals, and several cities have their own distinctive style.

regional.ja: 青森味噌カレー牛乳ラーメン
万代バスセンターのカレー

local: Japanese curry comes with pork, beef or chicken, and it is one of the most common home-cooked meals — every family has its own favorite ingredients. The best-known curry chain is CoCo Ichibanya, where you can choose the spice level and toppings.

shops.name: Shinjuku Nakamuraya Manna
shops.comment: The restaurant said to have served Japan's first Indian-style curry, in the early Showa era.

shops.name: Bondy Jimbocho Main Store
shops.query: ボンディ 神保町本店
shops.comment: A famous European-style curry shop in the bookstore district. Potatoes with butter come first.

shops.name: Kyoeido
shops.comment: A Jimbocho curry shop since the Taisho era, known for its dark, spicy Sumatra-style curry.

name: Sukiyaki
tagline: Beef simmered in a sweet soy broth
summary: Thin slices of beef, tofu and vegetables simmered at the table in a sweet soy sauce broth, then dipped in raw egg. It is a special-occasion dish, best with famous wagyu beef.
local: Many families also make sukiyaki at home for special occasions, such as New Year or celebrations.

shops.name: Ningyocho Imahan Main Store
shops.comment: A well-known sukiyaki restaurant using top wagyu. Staff cook the first pieces for you.

shops.name: Asakusa Imahan Main Store
shops.comment: A sukiyaki restaurant founded in the Meiji era. Lunch sets are a more affordable way to try it.

shops.name: Chinya Asakusa
shops.comment: Asakusa's oldest sukiyaki restaurant, founded in the Meiji era. It has its own butcher shop next door.

name: Shabu-shabu
tagline: Hot pot of thinly sliced meat
summary: Paper-thin slices of meat or fish swished through a pot of hot broth at the table, then dipped in sesame or ponzu sauce. Light and healthy, it shows off the quality of the ingredients.
local: Pork is the most common meat for shabu-shabu, especially at home, while restaurants also serve premium beef.

shops.name: Zakuro Muromachi
shops.comment: Zakuro is said to be the first restaurant to bring shabu-shabu to Tokyo. English menu available.

shops.name: Shabusen Ginza
shops.comment: A shabu-shabu restaurant from the same group as Zakuro, with counter seats and individual pots.
shops.access: Ginza Core building, near Ginza Station

shops.name: Kisoji
shops.comment: A shabu-shabu and sukiyaki chain with many branches in Tokyo. Good for families and groups.

name: Oden
tagline: Hearty one-pot stew, perfect in winter
summary: Daikon radish, boiled eggs, fish cakes, konjac and tofu simmered for hours in a light dashi broth and eaten with a dab of mustard. You can pick pieces one by one at convenience stores, food stalls and izakaya, and the broth and toppings change from region to region.

regional.ja: こんにゃく味噌おでん

local: In winter, convenience stores sell oden from a simmering pot by the counter, so you can pick your favorite pieces. Many families also buy the ingredients at the supermarket and make it at home.

shops.name: Otako Main Store
shops.query: お多幸 本店 日本橋
shops.comment: An oden restaurant since the Taisho era, with dark, rich Kanto-style broth. Try the tofu on rice.

shops.name: Otafuku Asakusa
shops.query: 浅草おでん 大多福
shops.comment: An oden restaurant in Asakusa since the Taisho era, known for its light, tasty broth.

shops.name: Convenience stores
shops.comment: In autumn and winter, almost every convenience store sells oden by the piece at the counter.

name: Tendon (tempura rice bowl)
tagline: Crispy tempura on a bowl of rice
summary: Shrimp, fish and vegetable tempura piled on a bowl of rice and drizzled with a sweet and savory soy-based sauce. The sauce soaks into the rice, making it a filling and affordable way to enjoy tempura.

shops.name: Kaneko Hannosuke Nihonbashi Main Store
shops.query: 日本橋 天丼 金子半之助
shops.comment: A very popular tendon shop with a huge, generous bowl. Expect a line.

shops.name: Daikokuya Tempura
shops.query: 大黒家天麩羅 浅草
shops.comment: An Asakusa tendon shop since the Meiji era, known for tempura soaked in a dark, sweet sauce.

shops.name: Dote no Iseya
shops.comment: A tendon shop in a historic wooden building, open since the Meiji era.

name: Gyudon (beef bowl)
tagline: Thin beef and onion simmered in a sweet sauce
summary: Thinly sliced beef and onion simmered in a sweet soy sauce broth and served over rice. Chain restaurants serve it fast and cheap all day, often with a raw egg, pickled ginger or miso soup on the side. Some regions are famous for pork or local wagyu versions.
local: Gyudon is one of the most widely eaten dishes in Japan, and most people eat it at chain restaurants — many office workers grab it for lunch. The big three chains, Sukiya, Yoshinoya and Matsuya, compete for the top spot, and everyone has a favorite. It is also made at home and sold at supermarkets and convenience stores.

shops.name: Yoshinoya Toyosu Market
shops.query: 吉野家 豊洲市場店
shops.comment: The successor to the famous Tsukiji No. 1 shop of Yoshinoya, the chain that made gyudon popular.

shops.name: Gyudon Sanbo
shops.query: 牛丼 サンボ 秋葉原
shops.comment: An old-school independent gyudon shop in Akihabara. Cash only.

shops.name: Matsuya
shops.comment: A big gyudon chain open early to late at many stations. Order from an English touch-screen machine.

name: Oyakodon (chicken and egg bowl)
tagline: Chicken and soft-cooked egg on rice
summary: Chicken and onion simmered in a sweet dashi and soy broth, then finished with softly set egg and served over rice. Its name means "parent and child" bowl, because it uses both chicken and egg. Restaurants using local free-range chicken make it extra special.
local: The Nakau chain is well known for oyakodon. It is also a common home-cooked dish and is sold at supermarkets and convenience stores.

shops.name: Tamahide
shops.comment: A chicken restaurant founded in the Edo period, said to be where oyakodon was born.

shops.name: Toritsune Shizendo
shops.query: 鳥つね 自然洞 湯島
shops.comment: A chicken specialist known for a rich, soft and creamy oyakodon.

shops.name: Torito (Tsukiji Outer Market)
shops.comment: A chicken shop in Tsukiji Outer Market serving oyakodon and chicken rice bowls.
shops.access: Tsukiji Outer Market, near Tsukiji Station

name: Kaisendon (seafood bowl)
tagline: Fresh sashimi on a bowl of rice
summary: A bowl of rice topped generously with fresh sashimi such as tuna, salmon, salmon roe and sea urchin. Fish markets and port towns serve the freshest bowls, and some let you choose your own toppings.
local: Almost every area famous for seafood has restaurants serving kaisendon, especially Hokkaido, Toyama, Ishikawa, Shizuoka and Kanagawa. In Tokyo, Toyosu Market has many restaurants serving it.

shops.name: Tsujihan Nihonbashi Main Store
shops.query: 日本橋 海鮮丼 つじ半
shops.comment: Famous for one 'luxury' bowl piled with chopped seafood, finished as sea bream rice in broth.

shops.name: Kaisendon Oedo (Tsukiji)
shops.query: 海鮮丼 大江戸 築地
shops.comment: A Tsukiji Outer Market shop with a long menu of seafood bowls.
shops.access: Tsukiji Outer Market, near Tsukiji Station

shops.name: Toyosu Senkyaku Banrai
shops.comment: A food hall next to Toyosu Market with many seafood bowl shops in one place.

name: Onigiri
tagline: Rice balls for a quick bite
summary: Rice shaped into a triangle or ball, often wrapped in seaweed and filled with salmon, pickled plum or tuna mayo. You can find them in every convenience store, and some regions have their own unique versions.

regional.ja: ポークたまごおにぎり

local: People often make onigiri at home or buy them at a shop and take them to work or school for lunch.

shops.name: Onigiri Asakusa Yadoroku
shops.comment: Said to be Tokyo's oldest onigiri shop, and listed in the Michelin Guide's Bib Gourmand.

shops.name: Bongo
shops.query: おにぎり ぼんご 大塚
shops.comment: Famous for big, loosely packed onigiri with lots of fillings. Lines can be very long.

shops.name: Convenience stores
shops.comment: Onigiri at 7-Eleven, FamilyMart and Lawson are cheap and good. Pull the numbered tabs to unwrap.

name: Miso soup
tagline: Comforting soup served with every meal
summary: A simple soup of dashi broth and miso (fermented soybean paste) with tofu, seaweed and green onion. It comes with almost every Japanese set meal, from breakfast at a hotel to a tonkatsu lunch. The type of miso and the ingredients change from region to region, and some local versions are hearty enough to be a meal on their own.
local: Miso soup is made at home almost every day in many Japanese families.

shops.name: Misogen Jiyugaoka
shops.query: 美噌元 自由が丘本店
shops.comment: A miso soup specialist where you can choose from soups made with miso from around Japan.

shops.name: MISOJYU Asakusa
shops.comment: A miso soup shop near Senso-ji, with set meals and onigiri. Good for breakfast.

shops.name: Otoya
shops.comment: A set-meal chain where every meal comes with rice and miso soup. A good way to try an everyday Japanese meal.

name: Unagi (grilled eel)
tagline: Eel grilled with a sweet soy glaze
summary: Freshwater eel grilled over charcoal and brushed with a sweet soy sauce glaze, served on rice. It is rich and tender, and Nagoya's hitsumabushi lets you enjoy it three different ways.

regional.ja: 柳川うなぎのせいろ蒸し

local: The most popular style is unaju, eel served on rice in a square lacquered box. Unadon comes in a bowl and tastes much the same, but usually has less eel. Kanto and Kansai grill eel differently: in the Kanto area it is steamed before grilling for a soft, fluffy texture, while in Kansai it is grilled directly for a crispier finish. Unaju is a luxury usually eaten at restaurants on special days, but beef bowl chains such as Sukiya, Matsuya and Yoshinoya offer more affordable unadon, mainly in summer.

shops.name: Nodaiwa Azabu Iikura Main Store
shops.query: 野田岩 麻布飯倉本店
shops.comment: An eel restaurant founded in the Edo period, known for wild eel in season.

shops.name: Obana
shops.comment: A famous eel restaurant serving unaju in a traditional tatami room. Expect a wait.

shops.name: Komagata Maekawa
shops.comment: An eel restaurant by the Sumida River since the Edo period, with river views.

name: Wagyu beef
tagline: Japan's famous marbled beef
summary: Japanese beef known for its fine marbling and melt-in-the-mouth texture. Each region raises its own brand of wagyu, enjoyed as steak, sukiyaki or yakiniku (grilled meat).

shops.name: Steak House Hama Roppongi
shops.query: ステーキハウス ハマ 六本木本店
shops.comment: Said to be one of the first teppanyaki steak houses. Chefs cook wagyu in front of you.

shops.name: Ginza Yoshizawa
shops.comment: A wagyu restaurant run by a butcher shop, serving sukiyaki and other beef dishes.

shops.name: Meat Yazawa
shops.query: ミート矢澤 五反田
shops.comment: A restaurant run by a meat wholesaler, famous for its wagyu hamburger steak.

name: Yakiniku (Japanese BBQ)
tagline: Grill your own meat at the table
summary: Bite-size cuts of beef and pork that you grill yourself over a charcoal or gas grill at the table, then dip in a sweet soy-based sauce. Restaurants range from cheap all-you-can-eat places to high-end wagyu specialists. Some regions grill lamb or chicken instead.
local: Many families also enjoy yakiniku at home, buying meat sliced for grilling at the supermarket and cooking it on a tabletop hot plate. Besides sweet soy-based sauce, salt-based sauces are also popular.

shops.name: Jojoen
shops.comment: A well-known yakiniku chain with many branches in Tokyo. Lunch sets are good value.

shops.name: Sumibiyakiniku Nakahara
shops.query: 炭火焼肉 なかはら 市ヶ谷
shops.comment: A top yakiniku restaurant known for rare cuts of wagyu. Book ahead.

shops.name: Yakiniku Toraji
shops.comment: A yakiniku chain with many branches in Tokyo, popular for its beef tongue.

name: Horumon (grilled offal)
tagline: Chewy, flavorful grilled offal
summary: Beef or pork offal such as intestine, tripe and heart, grilled over a fire and dipped in a garlicky miso or soy sauce. It is cheap, full of flavor and a favorite with locals at casual grill restaurants. Some towns even stir-fry it with noodles.

regional.ja: 厚木シロコロ・ホルモン

local: In Tokyo, the Kameido area is famous for its many horumon restaurants.

shops.name: Kameido Horumon Main Store
shops.query: 亀戸ホルモン 本店
shops.comment: The shop that started the horumon boom in Kameido. Very fresh offal grilled over charcoal.

shops.name: Horumon Masaru
shops.query: ホルモンまさる 三田
shops.comment: A horumon shop picked for Tabelog's Yakiniku Tokyo Top 100 list. Book ahead.

shops.name: Yamadaya (Mikawashima)
shops.comment: An old horumon shop in Mikawashima, known for very fresh offal.

name: Yakisoba
tagline: Stir-fried noodles with sauce
summary: Wheat noodles stir-fried with cabbage and pork in a tangy sauce, a staple at festivals and street stalls. Several towns are famous for their own local style.

regional.ja: 那須塩原スープ入り焼きそば

local: Yakisoba is also a common home-cooked meal. You can buy it ready-made at supermarkets and convenience stores, and instant cup yakisoba such as Nissin U.F.O. and Peyoung is very popular.

shops.name: Jimbocho Yakisoba Mikasa
shops.query: 神保町やきそば みかさ
shops.comment: A yakisoba-only shop with sauce and salt versions, topped with a soft-boiled egg.

shops.name: Apetito (Itabashi)
shops.query: あぺたいと 本店 板橋
shops.comment: Famous for yakisoba fried on both sides until crispy.

shops.name: Ichiban Hanten (Takadanobaba)
shops.query: 一番飯店 高田馬場
shops.comment: A long-running Chinese restaurant, known for its Shanghai-style yakisoba.

name: Wagashi & matcha sweets
ja: 和菓子・抹茶スイーツ
tagline: Traditional Japanese sweets
summary: Traditional sweets made from rice, sweet red bean paste and seasonal ingredients, often enjoyed with green tea. Kyoto is the place to try elegant wagashi and rich matcha desserts.

regional.ja: どじょう掬いまんじゅう

shops.name: Toraya Akasaka
shops.comment: A wagashi maker with about 500 years of history, famous for yokan. There is a cafe in the shop.

shops.name: Asakusa Umezono
shops.comment: A sweets cafe in Asakusa since the Edo period, known for awa-zenzai and anmitsu.

shops.name: Usagiya (Ueno)
shops.comment: A famous dorayaki shop. The pancakes are soft and the bean paste is freshly made.
